title: Who Will Sit on the Throne?
sum: King David is old and cannot get warm, and his court is splitting in two. Adonijah, the oldest living son, holds a feast with the army commander Joab and the priest Abiathar and is hailed as king. Nathan the prophet and Bathsheba go to David's bedside and remind him of an oath that Solomon would reign. David swears it again and orders Solomon anointed at once.

Zadok and Nathan anoint Solomon at the Gihon spring, the royal guard behind them, and the city roars. The noise reaches Adonijah's feast down the valley. His guests scatter, and Adonijah runs to the altar for safety. Solomon spares him, for now. The chapter ends the long story of David's family that began in 2 Samuel, and it leaves the reader asking how much was God's plan and how much was a palace plot.
readings: Read as God's choice

The LORD had loved Solomon from birth and named him through Nathan (2 Samuel 12:24–25). Chronicles says God told David that Solomon would build the temple and reign (1 Chronicles 22:9–10). On this reading Nathan acts as a prophet should: he makes sure the king keeps a promise that matches God's word, and the narrator shows God's will working through human means, as in the Joseph story.
Read as court intrigue

The oath is never recorded before Nathan suggests it, and Bathsheba repeats it word for word as he coached her. Readers such as R. N. Whybray and Robert Alter see a weak old king persuaded by a skillful prophet and an anxious mother, with the Jerusalem party (Zadok, Benaiah, the foreign guard) defeating the older Hebron party (Joab, Abiathar). The narrator lets the reader see the maneuvering without saying it was wrong.
Read as both

Many readers think the narrator wants both in view. God's purposes are carried out by people with mixed motives, just as in the stories of Jacob and Esau or of Joseph and his brothers (Genesis 50:20). The chapter neither hides the politics nor denies the providence.

views.H: The events took place about 970 BC. The details of place fit Jerusalem well: En-rogel and Gihon are both springs in the Kidron valley, half a mile apart, close enough for the shouting at one to be heard at the other. Rival heirs and a dying king's choice are common in ancient courts.
views.C: Since Leonhard Rost (1926), most critical scholars have read 1 Kings 1–2 as the end of a "Succession Narrative" or "Court History" that began in 2 Samuel 9–20. Some date it to Solomon's reign as a defense of his right to rule; others see it as later and quietly critical of the whole royal house.
views.A: No inscription mentions Solomon or Adonijah. But the pattern of a younger son put on the throne by his father and the court is known: the Assyrian Esarhaddon, a younger son, was chosen by Sennacherib and had to fight his brothers. Anointing of kings is also known from Hittite and Egyptian texts.
views.J: The rabbis noticed David's failure to discipline Adonijah (1:6) and drew the lesson for parents. They held that a king's son who inherits without dispute is not anointed, and that Solomon was anointed because Adonijah challenged him (Bavli Horayot 11b). Bathsheba is honored in Jewish tradition as a wise mother, and Proverbs 31:1–9 has been linked with her.
views.X: Christian readers have seen in Solomon's ride on David's mule into the city a picture of Jesus, the Son of David, riding into Jerusalem on a donkey (Matthew 21:1–9). Matthew's genealogy names Solomon's mother as "the wife of Uriah" (Matthew 1:6), keeping the hard memory alive.

deep.b:
The chapter sorts the court into two camps. With Adonijah: Joab, David's army commander since Hebron, and Abiathar, David's priest since the days of Saul (1 Samuel 22:20), along with the king's sons and the royal officials of Judah (1:9). With Solomon: Zadok the priest, who first appears in Samuel after the capture of Jerusalem (2 Samuel 8:17; Chronicles places a Zadok with David at Hebron, 1 Chronicles 12:28); Benaiah, who commanded the Kerethites and Pelethites, the foreign guard; Nathan the prophet; and "David's warriors" (1:8).

Historians often describe this as the old Hebron and Judah party against a new Jerusalem party. Bathsheba herself may have been from Jerusalem, and her grandfather may have been Ahithophel (2 Samuel 11:3; 2 Samuel 23:34). What decided the day was not the size of the feast at En-rogel but the king's word and the guard at Gihon.

Nathan tells Bathsheba to ask, "you swore an oath to your servant, didn't you?" (1:13), and then promises to come in and "make your words complete" (1:14). He also adds details she had not been told: that the guests were already shouting "Long live King Adonijah!" (1:25). The narrator records the plan and its success without a word of judgment. Readers who want a hero find one in Nathan, who also once had the courage to say "You are the man" to David (2 Samuel 12:7). Readers who want a cautionary tale find one in a court where a dying king can be steered. Both readings are as old as modern study of the book, and the text supports the question more than either answer.

echoes: 2 Samuel 3:2–5; 2 Samuel 12:24–25; 2 Samuel 15:1–12; 2 Samuel 4:9; 1 Chronicles 22:9–10; 1 Chronicles 28:5–7; Genesis 47:31; Exodus 21:13–14; Zechariah 9:9; Matthew 1:6; Matthew 21:1–9

settings.to: Bathsheba, Solomon's mother
settings.when: while Adonijah holds a feast to make himself king and David lies old in his room
settings.why: Nathan tells Bathsheba that her life and Solomon's are in danger, and gives her the words to say to David: "you swore an oath to your servant." He will come in and back her up. The plan works. The prophet who once condemned David over Bathsheba now acts to make her son king. Readers are left to wonder whether the oath was real, since we hear of it here for the first time.
views: Traditional readers think David had made the promise privately, perhaps after Solomon's birth, when the LORD loved the boy (2 Samuel 12:24–25).

Tomoo Ishida read the succession as a political struggle between two parties at court, and some scholars suspect Nathan and Bathsheba made up the oath. Even R. N. Whybray, who saw the story as written in support of Solomon, thought it frank about the court's maneuvers.

settings.what: Bathsheba and Nathan before the king
settings.to: King David, in his bedroom, with Abishag attending
settings.when: the same day, while Adonijah's guests shout "Long live King Adonijah!"
settings.why: Bathsheba reminds David of his oath, tells him all Israel is waiting for him to name his heir, and warns that she and Solomon will be treated as criminals. Nathan then asks whether David himself has made Adonijah king. The two speeches press a weak old king to act. They show how the succession was decided: not by the oldest son's claim, but by the king's word.

settings.what: David's oath and his order to anoint Solomon
settings.to: Bathsheba, then Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet and Benaiah
settings.when: at once, after Nathan's report
settings.why: David swears again that Solomon will reign. He orders the three men to put Solomon on David's own mule, anoint him at the Gihon spring, sound the horn, and seat him on the throne. Riding the king's mule and sitting on his throne showed the city that the old king had chosen. The order makes Solomon's rule lawful in the eyes of every reader who doubted it.

settings.by: Benaiah son of Jehoiada, commander of the royal guard
settings.to: King David
settings.when: when David orders Solomon anointed at Gihon
settings.why: Benaiah answers "Amen!" and prays that the LORD will be with Solomon as with David, and make his throne greater than David's. The captain of the guard is pledging the army's loyalty. His prayer also speaks the book's hope that the son will be greater than the father, which chapters 3–10 seem to fulfill.

settings.what: The courtiers' blessing and David's thanks
settings.by: David's servants, then David, as Jonathan son of Abiathar reports
settings.to: King David on his bed; David speaks to the LORD
settings.when: after Solomon is anointed and sits on the throne
settings.why: The servants pray that God will make Solomon's name and throne greater than David's, and David bows and blesses the LORD for letting him see his heir on the throne. Jonathan reports it to Adonijah's guests, and they scatter. The blessing shows that the old king and his court stand behind Solomon.

title: The Kingdom Made Firm
sum: On his deathbed David gives Solomon two kinds of advice. First, keep the law of Moses, and God will keep his promise to the house of David. Then, deal with Joab and Shimei, and be kind to the family of Barzillai. David dies after forty years as king.

Adonijah asks Bathsheba to get him Abishag as his wife. Solomon hears it as a bid for the throne and has him killed. He banishes the priest Abiathar to Anathoth, fulfilling the old word against Eli's house. Joab flees to the altar and is killed there. Shimei is confined to Jerusalem on pain of death and dies when he leaves to chase runaway slaves. The chapter begins and ends with the same claim: Solomon's kingdom was made secure.
readings: Read as justice

On this reading Solomon is carrying out the law and his father's charge. Joab had murdered two men in peacetime, and the law says such a killer has no refuge even at the altar (Exodus 21:14). Shimei had cursed the king and broke a fair agreement. Adonijah broke the terms on which he was spared. The guilt of innocent blood is removed from David's house (2:31–33).
Read as a purge

On this reading Solomon removes everyone who backed his rival, with legal reasons supplied after the fact. The pattern of a new king killing his brother and his brother's allies is common in the ancient world. The narrator's own aside, that Joab "had turned to follow Adonijah" (2:28), suggests the real reason. Walter Brueggemann and others read the chapter as an unflattering picture of how power is secured.
Read with the narrator's frame

The chapter is framed by "his kingdom grew very secure" (2:12) and "the kingdom was firm in Solomon's hand" (2:46). The narrator does not hide the blood, but places it inside God's promise to David (2:24, 2:33, 2:45). Many readers think the point is not to excuse Solomon but to show that God's promise moved forward through a very human king.

views.H: The reign began about 970 BC. The sequence of events, a deathbed charge, a rival's second move, a purge of the old guard and a reorganized court, fits what is known of royal successions in the ancient Near East.
views.C: Critical scholars generally see two hands in David's last speech: 2:2–4 in the language of Deuteronomy (the Deuteronomistic editors) and 2:5–9 from the older Court History. Some think the older story was written to defend Solomon's bloody start; others think it exposes it.
views.A: Gath, Achish and Philistine kings are known from excavation (Tell es-Safi) and inscriptions (the Ekron inscription names a later Achish). Altars with horns, like the one Adonijah and Joab grasped, have been found at Beersheba, Megiddo and elsewhere.
views.J: The rabbis debated Joab, praising his loyalty and his part in David's victories while admitting his murders (Bavli Sanhedrin 49a). They read David's charge about Shimei as a duty to answer a curse against the king.
views.X: Christian readers have often contrasted Solomon's securing of his kingdom by the sword with the kingdom of the Son of David, who told Peter to put away his sword (Matthew 26:52) and whose throne is secured by his own death. The queen mother at the king's right hand has been read in Catholic tradition as a type of Mary.

deep.b:
Adonijah (2:13–25). His request for Abishag may have been a claim to the throne, since taking the king's women was such a claim (2 Samuel 16:21–22), or it may have been a personal wish that gave Solomon his excuse. He had been warned (1:52).

Abiathar (2:26–27). Spared because he had carried the ark and shared David's hardships, he is sent home to Anathoth. The narrator presents this as the fulfillment of the word against Eli (1 Samuel 2:27–36).

Joab (2:28–34). He had murdered Abner and Amasa, and backed Adonijah. He is killed at the altar, which the law did not allow a deliberate murderer to use as a refuge (Exodus 21:14).

Shimei (2:36–46). He had cursed David and been spared by David's oath. Solomon gives him a test he can pass, and he fails it. The narrator records his crime and his promise, and lets the reader weigh them.

Fair readers can disagree about each case. What the chapter makes plain is that the peace of Solomon, whose name sounds like shalom, began with the sword.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Solomon finishes David's unfinished business
deep.b: My own reading: every death in chapter 2 matches a moment in 2 Samuel where David left justice undone or made a promise he could not keep. David cursed Joab for Abner's murder but said, "these men, Zeruiah's sons, are too harsh for me" (2 Samuel 3:39). He spared Shimei with an oath on the day of his return (2 Samuel 19:23). He never punished Amnon (2 Samuel 13:21) or corrected Adonijah (1:6). I suggest the narrator builds chapter 2 as a deliberate reversal: the son does with hard decisiveness everything the father failed to do, and the reader is left to decide whether that is wisdom or its absence. The wisdom Solomon asks for in chapter 3 is the wisdom to judge, and it comes only after this chapter's judgments. Commentators have often noted that David's charge looks back to old wrongs; reading the whole chapter as a mirror of David's failures is my own proposal.

echoes: Joshua 23:14; Deuteronomy 17:18–20; 2 Samuel 7:11–16; 2 Samuel 3:27–39; 2 Samuel 20:8–10; 2 Samuel 16:5–13; 2 Samuel 19:16–23; 2 Samuel 19:31–39; 1 Samuel 2:27–36; Exodus 21:14; Numbers 35:33; Psalm 110:1

settings.to: his son Solomon, the new king
settings.when: when David's days are nearly over
settings.why: David first tells Solomon to be strong and to keep the law of Moses, so that God's promise of a lasting throne will stand. Then he names unfinished business: Joab must not die in peace, Barzillai's sons must be cared for, and Shimei must not go unpunished. The charge holds both the faith of Deuteronomy and the hard politics of a royal court. It gives Solomon reasons for the deaths that follow.
views: Many critical scholars think verses 2–4, in the language of Deuteronomy (compare Joshua 1:7–8), were added by the historian, while verses 5–9 belong to the older court story.
Scholars who read the Court History as royal apology see the charge as a way to show that Solomon's purge was ordered by David, not done for his own gain.

settings.to: Bathsheba, the king's mother
settings.when: after David's death
settings.why: Adonijah admits the kingdom went to his brother "from the LORD," then asks for David's young attendant Abishag as his wife. In the ancient world, taking a dead king's woman could be a claim to his throne (compare 2 Samuel 16:21–22). Whether he meant it so or not, the request gives Solomon a reason to act.

settings.to: Bathsheba, his mother, at the throne
settings.when: when she brings Adonijah's request
settings.why: Solomon says she might as well ask the kingdom for Adonijah, and swears by the LORD that his brother will die that day. He grounds his oath in God's gift of a house to him. The scene shows the new king securing his throne, and readers must decide how much was justice and how much was fear.

settings.to: Abiathar the priest, who had backed Adonijah
settings.when: after Adonijah's death
settings.why: Solomon sends Abiathar home to Anathoth and removes him from the priesthood, sparing his life because he carried the ark and shared David's hardships. The narrator says this fulfilled the word against Eli's house at Shiloh (1 Samuel 2:27–36). Readers see an old prophecy come true through a political decision. Anathoth was also Jeremiah's town (Jeremiah 1:1).

settings.to: Benaiah, captain of the guard
settings.when: when Joab clings to the horns of the altar in the LORD's tent
settings.why: Solomon orders Joab killed even at the altar, to take away from David's house the blood Joab shed when he murdered Abner and Amasa. The law allowed a murderer to be taken even from the altar (Exodus 21:14). The order frees the throne of bloodguilt, which David's own curse had put on Joab (2 Samuel 3:28–29).

settings.to: Shimei son of Gera, the Benjaminite who cursed David
settings.when: after Joab's death
settings.why: Solomon orders Shimei to build a house in Jerusalem and never cross the Kidron Valley, on pain of death, and Shimei agrees under oath. The order keeps a possible leader of Saul's tribe under the king's eye. It also gives him a way to live, if he keeps the terms.

settings.to: Shimei, called before the king
settings.when: three years later, after Shimei leaves Jerusalem to bring back runaway slaves from Gath
settings.why: Solomon reminds Shimei of his oath and of the harm he did David, and declares that the LORD is turning it back on his head, while Solomon's throne stands. Shimei dies. The chapter ends, "Now the kingdom was firm in Solomon's hand." Readers see a throne made secure, and must weigh how it was done.

traditions.q: Is the queen mother seated at Solomon's right hand (1 Kings 2:19) a picture of Mary?
views: Many Catholic teachers say yes. In Judah the king's mother was the great lady of the court who brought requests to her son, and Mary, mother of the Son of David, is honored as Queen and asked to pray for her children (Catechism 966; Scott Hahn, Hail, Holy Queen, 2001).
The Orthodox call Mary Queen and ask her prayers in every service, and their hymns apply Psalm 45 to her. They draw this honor from the liturgy and the fathers more than from the figure of Bathsheba.

Lutherans honor Mary as the mother of God, but the Augsburg Confession says Scripture does not teach calling on the saints, since Christ is the one mediator (article 21). The queen mother belongs to Solomon's court history, not to teaching about Mary.

No. Baptists read the scene as a court custom, and point out that Solomon refused the request Bathsheba brought (1 Kings 2:22–24). Believers come to God through Christ alone, with no other go-between (1 Timothy 2:5).

title: A Heart That Listens
sum: Solomon marries Pharaoh's daughter and worships at the high places, as everyone did before the temple was built. At the great shrine of Gibeon he offers a thousand burnt offerings, and that night the LORD appears to him in a dream: "Ask. What should I give you?" Solomon asks for "a heart that listens," to judge God's people and tell good from bad. God is pleased, and promises riches and glory as well, and long life if Solomon walks in his ways.

Then comes the proof. Two prostitutes bring the king a case with no witnesses: two babies were born, one died, and each mother claims the living one. Solomon calls for a sword and orders the child cut in two. The real mother begs him to give the child away rather than kill him, and the king gives him to her. All Israel sees that God's wisdom is in him to do justice.
readings: Read as the model of a good king

The chapter shows the ideal: a king who knows he is small, asks God for what his people need rather than what he wants, and uses his gift first for the weakest people in the land. Jewish and Christian teachers have used the dream as a model of prayer.
Read with the warnings

The chapter's first verses hold quiet warnings: an Egyptian marriage, high places, and the word "only" (3:2–3). God's promise of long life has a condition (3:14). Readers who know chapter 11 see the seeds of Solomon's fall planted even here.
Read as wisdom literature

The two stories, dream and court case, belong together: wisdom is asked for, given, and shown. The king's test works because it understands a mother's love (3:26). Wisdom in the Bible is practical insight into people, not only learning.

views.H: Gibeon was the leading shrine before the temple, and Chronicles explains that the tabernacle stood there (2 Chronicles 1:3–6). The marriage alliance with Egypt fits the weakened 21st dynasty, which may have given Gezer as a dowry (9:16).
views.C: Many scholars compare the dream to Egyptian and Mesopotamian royal dream reports, which legitimized a king. The judgment of the two mothers is a widespread folk tale attached to the most famous wise king. The comments on the high places (3:2–3) come from the Deuteronomistic editors.
views.A: Royal dream texts such as the Dream Stele of Thutmose IV (about 1400 BC) and the cylinders of Gudea of Lagash (about 2100 BC) show kings receiving promises or plans from gods in dreams. An Amarna letter shows that Egyptian princesses were not given to foreign kings in the 14th century BC, which makes Solomon's marriage notable.
views.J: The rabbis praised Solomon's request and taught that he asked for wisdom because everything else follows from it (Midrash Song of Songs Rabbah 1:1). The Talmud counts Solomon's court among three places where a voice from heaven confirmed a verdict, saying "She is his mother" (Bavli Makkot 23b). Rashi reads "youngster" as twelve years old.
views.X: Christians have read the dream with Jesus' teaching to seek God's kingdom first (Matthew 6:33) and James's promise that God gives wisdom to all who ask (James 1:5).

deep.h: The two mothers and the folk tale
deep.b:
Stories of a judge who finds a child's true mother by a test are told in India (a Buddhist Jataka tale in which the women pull the child across a line), China (the drama The Chalk Circle), and many other places; Hugo Gressmann collected more than twenty in 1907. The biblical story is the oldest written version known. It is impossible to say whether it is the source of the others or one telling of a wider tale.

What the Bible's version stresses is its frame. It follows directly on Solomon's prayer for "a heart that listens" to "judge your people" (3:9), and it ends with the people seeing "God's wisdom" in him "for doing justice" (3:28). The petitioners are prostitutes, the least respected people in the city, and they have the same right to the king's justice as anyone. The king's genius is to set up a test in which love reveals itself.

echoes: 2 Chronicles 1:1–13; Deuteronomy 17:16–17; Genesis 41:7; 2 Samuel 14:17; Psalm 72:1–4; Proverbs 3:13–16; Isaiah 11:2–4; Matthew 6:33; James 1:5; 1 Corinthians 1:24

settings.what: The dream at Gibeon: Solomon asks for wisdom
settings.to: Solomon, and the LORD, in a dream at night
settings.when: after Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings at the great high place at Gibeon, early in his reign
settings.why: God says "Ask," and the young king asks for "a heart that listens," to judge God's people and tell good from bad. God gives him wisdom, and adds riches and honor, and promises long life if he walks in God's ways. The scene teaches that a king's power is for justice, and that wisdom is God's gift. The last "if" warns readers who know how Solomon's reign will end (11:1–13).

settings.what: The case of the two mothers
settings.to: King Solomon, sitting as judge
settings.when: soon after the dream at Gibeon
settings.why: Two prostitutes who share a house each claim the living baby. With no witnesses, Solomon calls for a sword and orders the child cut in two. The true mother gives up her claim to save his life, and the king gives her the child. The case proves to all Israel that God's wisdom is in the king. It also shows that justice reached even the lowest in the land.
views: Traditional readers take it as a case from Solomon's court.
Hugo Gressmann and others found similar stories of a wise judge and two mothers in India and elsewhere. They think a well-known tale was told of Solomon to show his wisdom.

title: Like the Sand by the Sea
sum: The chapter is a portrait of a working kingdom. It lists Solomon's chief officials, then twelve district officers who each supply the court for one month of the year. It describes the king's daily provisions, his horses and his dominion "from the River" to the border of Egypt.

Then it describes the people: as many as the sand by the sea, eating, drinking and glad, each one safe under his own vine and fig tree from Dan to Beersheba. Finally it praises Solomon's wisdom as greater than all the east and Egypt: three thousand proverbs, a thousand and five songs, and knowledge of trees and animals, birds and fish. People come from every nation to hear him. In the Hebrew Bible, 4:21–34 is numbered 5:1–14.
readings: Read as the promises fulfilled

The language deliberately echoes God's promises to Abraham: people like the sand (Genesis 22:17), borders from Egypt to the Euphrates (Genesis 15:18), and rest from enemies. Solomon's reign is the high point of Israel's story.
Read with an eye on the cost

The same chapter describes a growing state: officials, taxes in kind, a draft labor system (4:6), many horses (4:26). Samuel had warned that a king would take the people's sons and harvests (1 Samuel 8:11–17), and the northern tribes will complain of Solomon's "heavy yoke" (12:4).
Read as wisdom on display
The list of districts and provisions shows wisdom as good government; the closing verses show it as learning and art. Both belong to the biblical idea of a wise king (Proverbs 25:2).

views.H: Traditional readers take the lists as drawn from royal archives (11:41) and the summary of dominion as describing a real network of vassal states, possible in the 10th century BC when Egypt and Assyria were weak.
views.C: Many critical scholars see a mix: some lists (the officials and districts) may come from old records, while the sweeping summaries (4:20–21, 4:24–25) are later idealization. The phrase "Beyond the River" (4:24) is often taken as a sign of writing from a Babylonian or Persian viewpoint.
views.A: The size of Solomon's kingdom is one of the most debated questions in biblical archaeology. The debate turns on 10th-century Jerusalem (how big?), on the gates and palaces at Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer (Solomon's, or a century later?), and on radiocarbon dating. See the deep dive below and the topic on the united monarchy debate.
views.J: Jewish tradition made Solomon the author of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, and later legend made him master of animals, demons and the shamir worm. The verse about the vine and fig tree became a picture of messianic peace (Micah 4:4).
views.X: Christian readers see in the nations coming to hear Solomon (4:34) a picture of the nations coming to Christ, "something more than Solomon" (Matthew 12:42), in whom "all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden" (Colossians 2:3).

deep.h: How big was Solomon's kingdom? Three views
deep.b:
The traditional view. Scholars such as Kenneth Kitchen and the authors of A Biblical History of Israel (Provan, Long and Longman) argue that a kingdom like the one described is entirely possible. In the 10th century there was a gap in great-power politics: Egypt was divided and Assyria had not yet expanded west. Small states could grow quickly under strong rulers, and the Bible's lists of officials and districts look like real records. Lack of inscriptions is normal for this period and region.

The minimalist view. Scholars such as Niels Peter Lemche and Thomas Thompson have argued that the united monarchy is largely a later literary creation. Israel Finkelstein, with a different method, argues that Jerusalem in the 10th century was a small highland settlement and that the large building projects once credited to Solomon belong to the 9th-century kings of the northern kingdom, especially the Omrides.

The middle view. Amihai Mazar, William Dever and others hold that David and Solomon ruled a real state centered on Jerusalem, smaller and simpler than the summaries suggest, but with monumental building (such as the Stepped Stone Structure in the City of David) and real influence beyond the hills. Finds such as Khirbet Qeiyafa, a fortified town of about 1000 BC identified by its excavators as Judahite (others, such as Israel Finkelstein and Nadav Na'aman, contest this), are often cited in support.

In the 1950s and 60s Yigael Yadin noticed that the city gates at Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer had the same six-chambered plan, and he connected them with 9:15, which says Solomon built those three cities. For a generation these "Solomonic gates" were textbook evidence for the united monarchy. Since the 1990s the link has been questioned. Finkelstein's "low chronology" redates the levels a century later, to the 9th century; others note that six-chambered gates were built over a long period and in places Solomon never ruled, and that the Megiddo gate may belong to a later level than the palaces near it. Excavators at Gezer and Hazor (Dever, Amnon Ben-Tor) have defended a 10th-century date, and radiocarbon results have been read both ways. The question is still open. 9:15 itself belongs to the next part of this book; the full discussion is on the topic page.

echoes: Genesis 15:18; Genesis 22:17; 1 Samuel 8:11–17; 2 Samuel 8:16–18; 2 Samuel 20:23–26; Deuteronomy 17:16; Micah 4:4; Zechariah 3:10; Psalm 72:8; Proverbs 1:1; Proverbs 22:17–24:22; Matthew 12:42

title: Cedar from Lebanon
sum: Hiram, king of Tyre and an old friend of David, sends envoys to the new king. Solomon answers with a plan: his father could not build a house for the LORD because of his wars, but now there is peace on every side, and Solomon will build the house God promised David's son would build. He asks Hiram for cedar from Lebanon and skilled Sidonian woodcutters.

Hiram agrees. His men will float the logs down the coast in rafts, and Solomon will pay with wheat and oil every year. The two kings make a treaty. Then Solomon drafts thirty thousand Israelites to work in Lebanon in shifts, and puts tens of thousands more to carrying loads and cutting great stones in the hills. In the Hebrew Bible this chapter is 5:15–32.
readings: Read as the promise to David coming true

Solomon quotes the promise of 2 Samuel 7:13 and claims the rest from enemies that Deuteronomy said would come before the chosen place was built (Deuteronomy 12:10–11). The chapter shows the nations, in the person of Hiram, helping to build the LORD's house.
Read as the price of glory

The same chapter introduces the labor draft. The thirty thousand men from "all Israel" (5:13) foreshadow the complaint that breaks the kingdom (12:4). Readers who follow Samuel's warning about kings (1 Samuel 8) see the cost of the temple paid by ordinary families.

views.H: Tyre was the leading Phoenician city of the 10th century, and Josephus quotes Tyrian records naming Hiram son of Abibaal as Solomon's contemporary. Cedar from Lebanon was the timber of choice for temples across the ancient Near East.
views.C: Critical scholars generally accept the alliance with Tyre as historical, while debating the numbers of workers and the scale of the project. The two accounts of forced labor (5:13–14 and 9:20–22) are often taken as from different sources or editors.
views.A: Egyptian texts like the Story of Wenamun describe buying cedar from Byblos (Gebal), and Assyrian reliefs from Sargon II's palace show Phoenician ships moving logs. Fine ashlar masonry in Phoenician style appears in royal buildings in Israel.
views.J: Jewish tradition admired Hiram as a friend of Israel, though some rabbis criticized him for later claiming to be a god (Ezekiel 28:2, which they applied to him).
views.X: Christian writers have seen in Hiram, a foreign king who brings materials for God's house, a picture of the nations bringing their glory into the new Jerusalem (Isaiah 60:13; Revelation 21:24–26).

deep.b: Kings gives three groups: 30,000 men drafted "out of all Israel" who took turns in Lebanon (5:13–14); 70,000 carriers and 80,000 stonecutters (5:15); and 3,300 foremen (5:16). Chronicles says the 150,000 were resident foreigners in Israel (2 Chronicles 2:17–18), and 9:20–22 says Solomon made slaves only of the remaining Canaanites. Many readers resolve this by distinguishing a rotating draft of Israelites (one month in three) from permanent forced labor by non-Israelites. Others think the sources simply disagree, one remembering Solomon's burden on Israel and the other softening it. When the northern tribes ask Rehoboam to lighten their "heavy yoke" (12:4) and stone the officer over the forced labor (12:18), the reader sees which memory they kept.

echoes: 2 Samuel 5:11; 2 Samuel 7:1–13; 1 Chronicles 22:8; Deuteronomy 12:10–11; 2 Chronicles 2:1–18; 9:20–22; 12:4; 1 Samuel 8:11–17; Ezra 3:7; Amos 1:9

settings.to: Hiram, king of Tyre, through messengers
settings.when: after Hiram sends greetings on Solomon's accession
settings.why: Solomon explains that David could not build the LORD's house because of war. God has now given rest, and Solomon means to build it as God promised David (2 Samuel 7:13). He asks for cedars from Lebanon and offers to pay Hiram's workers. The letter presents the temple as the fulfillment of Nathan's oracle, built in peace. It also shows Solomon dealing as an equal with a foreign king.

settings.to: King Solomon
settings.when: on receiving Solomon's request
settings.why: Hiram blesses the LORD for giving David a wise son, agrees to float cedar and cypress down the coast in rafts, and asks for food for his household in return. A foreign king praises Israel's God, which fits the book's picture of Solomon's fame (4:34). The trade deal also shows how much the temple depended on foreign skill.

settings.to: thirty thousand men drafted out of all Israel, in shifts of ten thousand a month; the text lists separately seventy thousand carriers and eighty thousand stonecutters
settings.when: while the temple is being prepared
settings.why: Solomon orders forced labor to cut timber in Lebanon and stone in the hills. The order bound Israelite men to work for the king one month in three. It answered the problem of how to build on a grand scale, but it fulfilled Samuel's warning that a king would take their sons (1 Samuel 8:11–17). The tribes later complained of this "heavy yoke" (12:4) and stoned the man in charge (12:18).
views: 9:22 says Solomon made no Israelite a slave, while this passage says he drafted men from all Israel. Many readers think the draft here was temporary labor, different from the lasting slavery of the Canaanite peoples. Others see two sources that do not fully agree.

title: A House for the LORD
sum: Four hundred and eighty years after the exodus, in the fourth year of his reign, Solomon begins the LORD's house. The chapter is an architect's report: a building sixty cubits long, with a porch in front, a great hall, and at the back a cube-shaped inner room, the most holy place. Three stories of side rooms wrap around it. The stone was cut at the quarry, so no iron tool was heard on the site.

In the middle of the measurements the LORD speaks: if Solomon keeps his commands, God will dwell among the Israelites and not abandon them. Then the description moves inside: cedar walls carved with gourds, flowers, palm trees and cherubim, everything covered with gold, and two great olive-wood cherubim whose wings fill the inner room from wall to wall. The work takes seven years.
readings: Read as the place where heaven meets earth

For Jewish and Christian readers alike, the temple is the place God chose to put his name and meet his people. Its carvings of cherubim, palms and flowers make it a garden like Eden, and its inner room is the throne room of the invisible King.
Read as a royal building
Historians compare the plan to other temples of the region and note that it stood beside the palace as a royal chapel. The king who builds a god's house is a familiar figure in ancient inscriptions.
Read with the condition

The LORD's word in 6:11–13 makes clear that the building does not guarantee God's presence. Jeremiah will say the same to people who trusted in "The LORD's temple, the LORD's temple, the LORD's temple" (Jeremiah 7:4).

views.H: The temple was begun about 966 BC and finished about 959 BC. Its three-part plan, side rooms, and cherubim fit what is known of temples in the region in this period.
views.C: Many scholars think the building account draws on a temple record or archive, perhaps from later repairs, and that 6:11–13, missing in the Greek, is a later addition in Deuteronomy's language. The date of 480 years is often taken as a scheme of twelve generations.
views.A: No remains of Solomon's temple have been excavated; the Temple Mount cannot be dug. The closest parallels are the temples at 'Ain Dara in Syria and Tell Tayinat in Turkey, and the Israelite temple at Motza near Jerusalem. Phoenician ivories and Assyrian art show cherub-like winged figures and palm designs like those described.
views.J: Jewish tradition holds the temple as the dwelling of the Shekhinah, God's presence, and still mourns its destruction on the fast of Tisha b'Av. The rabbis told of the shamir worm that cut the stones in silence. Synagogues face toward the site of the most holy place.
views.X: The New Testament calls Jesus' body the temple (John 2:19–21), the church God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22), and pictures the new Jerusalem as a cube, like the most holy place, with no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple (Revelation 21:16, 21:22).

deep.h: The temple in cubits and feet
deep.b:
Assuming the common cubit of about 18 inches (45 centimeters):

  • The house: 60 by 20 cubits, 30 high, about 90 by 30 feet, 45 high (27 by 9 by 13.5 meters) (6:2).
  • The porch: 20 cubits wide, 10 deep, about 30 by 15 feet (9 by 4.5 meters) (6:3).
  • The great hall: 40 cubits long, about 60 feet (18 meters) (6:17).
  • The inner room: a cube of 20 cubits, about 30 feet (9 meters) each way (6:20).
  • The side rooms: three stories, 5, 6 and 7 cubits wide, each 5 cubits high, about 7.5, 9 and 10.5 feet wide (6:6, 6:10).
  • The cherubim: 10 cubits high, with wingspans of 10 cubits each, about 15 feet (4.5 meters) (6:23–24).

If the longer royal cubit (about 20.5 inches, 52 centimeters) was used, add about one seventh to each figure.

echoes: Exodus 25–27; Exodus 20:25; 2 Samuel 7:5–13; 2 Chronicles 3:1–14; Ezekiel 40–43; Jeremiah 7:4–15; John 2:19–21; 1 Corinthians 3:16; Hebrews 9:1–7; Revelation 21:16–22

settings.what: The LORD's word during the building
settings.to: Solomon
settings.when: while the temple is being built
settings.why: God tells Solomon that the house is not enough. If he keeps God's laws, God will keep his word to David and live among Israel and not leave them. Set in the middle of building details, the word warns readers that God's presence depends on obedience, not on walls and gold. For exiles who had seen the temple burned, it explained why.

title: Palace, Pillars and the Sea
sum: The chapter opens with Solomon's own buildings: thirteen years of work on a palace complex that included the House of the Forest of Lebanon with its rows of cedar pillars, a porch of pillars, a throne room where he judged, his own house, and a house for Pharaoh's daughter, all of great cut stones.

Then Solomon brings a second Hiram from Tyre, a master bronze worker with an Israelite mother. He casts the two great pillars, Jakin and Boaz, for the temple porch; the Sea, a huge round basin standing on twelve bronze oxen; ten bronze stands on wheels, each with its basin; and all the bronze pots, shovels and bowls, cast in clay molds in the Jordan valley. Solomon makes the gold furnishings himself, and brings David's dedicated treasure into the temple storerooms.
readings: Read as the glory of the house

The bronze and gold describe a house fit for a king, and the king is the LORD. The pillars, the Sea and the stands all have symbolic depth: stability, the waters of chaos tamed, the twelve tribes standing around God's presence.
Read with the thirteen years

Readers ancient and modern have noticed that the palace took thirteen years, the temple seven, and that the narrator puts the palace in the middle of the temple account. Some read a quiet criticism of a king more devoted to his own house; others think the palace simply was larger.

views.H: The bronze work required real expertise in casting very large objects, which Phoenician craftsmen had. The Jordan valley near Succoth has evidence of ancient metalworking, and the clay there suits molds.
views.C: Critical scholars see a detailed source behind 7:13–51, perhaps a temple inventory, and note that the Greek places the palace section (7:1–12) after 7:51, which may be the older order. The technical terms of the stands are among the hardest in the Hebrew Bible.
views.A: Bronze wheeled stands from Cyprus, free-standing pillars at the doors of temples at 'Ain Dara and Tell Tayinat, and Herodotus's description of twin pillars at the temple of Melqart in Tyre all help to picture what Hiram made. The Arch of Titus shows a later temple's lampstand.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition explained the pillars' names, and medieval Jewish commentators worked to reconcile the measures with Chronicles. The Talmud takes the Sea's ten-and-thirty measure as the rule for a circle (Bavli Eruvin 14a), and later tradition found a value close to pi in the written form of the word "line" (7:23).
views.X: Medieval Christian writers such as Bede saw in the Sea a picture of baptism and in the twelve oxen the twelve apostles. Revelation's "sea of glass" before God's throne (Revelation 4:6) is often linked with it.

deep.h: The bronze work in feet and gallons
deep.b:
• Each pillar: 18 cubits high and 12 around, about 27 feet high (8 meters) and nearly 6 feet (1.8 meters) thick; capitals 5 cubits (7.5 feet, 2.3 meters) (7:15–16).
  • The Sea: 10 cubits across, 5 high, 30 around, about 15 feet across and 7.5 feet high (4.5 by 2.3 meters); holding 2,000 baths, about 11,600 gallons (44,000 liters) (7:23–26).
  • Each stand: 4 by 4 cubits, 3 high, about 6 by 6 by 4.5 feet (1.8 by 1.8 by 1.35 meters), with wheels 1.5 cubits (27 inches, 68 centimeters) high (7:27–32).
  • Each basin: 40 baths, about 230 gallons (880 liters), 4 cubits (6 feet) across (7:38).

Measures are approximate: the cubit was about 18 inches (45 centimeters), the bath about 22 liters.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the bronze world around the house
deep.b: My own suggestion: the bronze objects in the courtyard form a small picture of the world as the Hebrew Bible imagines it. The Sea stands for the waters God tamed at creation (Genesis 1:9–10; Psalm 104:6–9). Its twelve oxen face the four directions like the tribes around the tabernacle (Numbers 2), so Israel holds up the tamed sea. The ten stands with their basins carry water on wheels, as the clouds carry rain (Job 37:11–13). And the two pillars at the door, "he establishes" and "in him is strength," recall the pillars on which God set the earth (1 Samuel 2:8; Psalm 75:3). The worshiper crossing the courtyard walks through a world in order on the way to the throne room. Scholars such as Jon Levenson, Carol Meyers and Gregory Beale have argued that the temple was a small cosmos; the specific mapping of each object here is my own proposal.
deep.refs: 7:15–39; Genesis 1:9–10; Psalm 104:6–9; Numbers 2; Job 37:11–13; 1 Samuel 2:8; Psalm 75:3

echoes: 2 Chronicles 2:13–14; 2 Chronicles 3:15–4:22; Exodus 31:1–6; Exodus 25:23–40; Exodus 30:17–21; Jeremiah 52:17–23; 2 Kings 16:17; 2 Kings 25:13–17; Revelation 4:6

title: The Cloud Fills the House
sum: In the seventh month, at the Feast of Booths, all Israel gathers. The priests carry the ark of the covenant up from the City of David into the inner room, under the cherubim's wings, with nothing inside it but the two stone tablets of Moses. As the priests come out, a cloud fills the house, and the glory of the LORD is so heavy that they cannot stay to serve.

Solomon blesses the people and tells how God kept his word to David. Then, hands raised to the heavens, he prays. No house can contain God, he says, not even the highest heavens; yet let God's eyes be open to this place and hear the prayers made toward it. He lists seven cases, from a disputed oath to defeat, drought, plague, the prayer of a foreigner, war, and exile in a far land, and in each asks God to hear from heaven and forgive. The festival ends after two weeks of sacrifice and feasting, and the people go home glad.
readings: Read as a prayer for every age

The prayer is written so that later readers can use it: in war, famine, guilt, or exile, they can turn toward God's house and be heard. For Jews after the temple fell, it made prayer itself the center of worship.
Read as the high point of Kings
With the ark at rest and the glory in the house, every promise seems fulfilled: rest, a chosen place, a son of David on the throne (8:20, 8:56). Everything after this is measured against this day.
Read with the exile in view

The longest case is exile (8:46–53). Many scholars think the prayer was shaped for readers in Babylon. On either view, the prayer gives those far from the land a way back: if they "turn back and plead for grace" and pray "facing their land," God will hear (8:47–48).

views.H: The dedication took place about 959 BC, at the autumn festival. Dedication ceremonies with sacrifice, prayer and feasting are known from royal inscriptions of the time; Solomon's prayer is unusual in its humility before a God no house can hold.
views.C: Most critical scholars see the speeches (8:14–61) as composed or heavily shaped by the Deuteronomistic writers, with the short poem of 8:12–13 as one of the oldest pieces in the book. The Greek's placement of that poem, citing "the Book of the Song," may point to an ancient source.
views.A: Ancient Near Eastern temple dedications, such as Gudea's for Ningirsu and Assyrian royal inscriptions, include processions of the god's symbol, feasts and large numbers of sacrifices. Ashurnasirpal II claimed to have fed 69,574 guests at the dedication of his palace at Kalhu.
views.J: Parts of this chapter are read in synagogues as haftarot: 8:2–21 on the second day of Sukkot and 8:54–66 on Shemini Atzeret. Jews pray facing Jerusalem on the basis of this prayer (Bavli Berakhot 30a), and its confession, "We have sinned, we have gone wrong, we have done evil," shaped the Day of Atonement liturgy.
views.X: Stephen quotes the idea that the Most High does not make his home in what hands have made (Acts 7:48–50). John's Gospel presents Jesus as the place where God's glory dwells among his people (John 1:14) and his body as the temple (John 2:19–21). Christians also hear in the welcome of foreigners (8:41–43) the hope of a a house of prayer for all the peoples (Mark 11:17).

deep.h: The seven cases of the prayer
deep.b:
1. An oath of innocence at the altar (8:31–32).
  2. Defeat in battle because of sin (8:33–34).
  3. Drought because of sin (8:35–36).
  4. Famine, plague, pests or siege (8:37–40).
  5. The foreigner who comes to pray (8:41–43).
  6. Israel at war, praying toward the city (8:44–45).
  7. Exile in an enemy land (8:46–53).

Each case ends with a request that God "hear in the heavens" and act or forgive. Most of the disasters are the curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. The prayer turns those curses into occasions for turning back to God, and it ends with Israel's oldest claim on God: "They are your people ... You brought them out of Egypt" (8:51).

deep.h: Can God live in a house?
deep.b: Solomon calls the house "a settled place for you to live forever" (8:13), and then asks, "can God truly make his home on earth?" (8:27). The prayer holds both: God is in the heavens and cannot be contained; God has also put his name in this place and promised to watch over it (8:29). Scholars have called this "name theology," a way of speaking of God's presence without making him a prisoner of his temple. It prepared Israel to survive the temple's destruction, as Jon Levenson argued in his essay "From Temple to Synagogue." Jews pray toward the place where it stood; Christians speak of God dwelling in Christ and in his people. The question Solomon asked remains one of the Bible's great questions.

echoes: Exodus 40:34–35; 2 Samuel 7:1–16; Deuteronomy 12:5–11; Deuteronomy 28; Leviticus 26; 2 Chronicles 5:2–7:10; Psalm 132; Isaiah 56:6–7; Isaiah 66:1; Daniel 6:10; Daniel 9:4–19; Acts 7:47–50; John 1:14; John 2:19–21

settings.what: Solomon's words as the cloud fills the house
settings.to: the LORD, in the hearing of the priests and the assembly
settings.when: when the ark is placed in the inner room and the cloud of the LORD's glory fills the temple
settings.why: Solomon says the LORD has chosen to live in thick darkness, and that he has built him a settled place forever. The short poem links the temple to the cloud that filled the tabernacle in the wilderness (Exodus 40:34–35). Its claim of "forever" is answered in his own prayer, which asks whether God can live on earth at all (8:27).

settings.what: Solomon blesses the assembly of Israel
settings.to: the whole assembly of Israel, standing in the temple courts
settings.when: at the Feast of Booths in the seventh month, at the dedication
settings.why: Solomon blesses the LORD for keeping his word to David: God chose Jerusalem and David, and David's son has built the house for God's name. The speech presents the temple as the fulfillment of 2 Samuel 7, and teaches the people that the house holds God's "name," not God himself.

settings.what: Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple
settings.to: the LORD, God of Israel, with hands spread toward heaven, before the altar and all the assembly
settings.when: at the dedication of the temple
settings.why: Solomon asks God to keep his promise to David, admits that even the highest heavens cannot hold him, and asks him to hear prayers made toward this house. He lists seven cases. They are an oath in court, defeat in war, drought, famine and plague, the foreigner who comes to pray, an army at war, and captivity in an enemy land. In each, he asks God to hear from heaven and forgive. The last case pictures Israel carried off and praying toward the land and the temple, saying "We have sinned." For the exiles in Babylon, that was their exact situation, and the prayer told them God could still hear them far from the temple. It shaped the Jewish practice of praying toward Jerusalem (compare Daniel 6:10).
views: Traditional readers take the prayer as Solomon's, with its last cases foreseeing what could happen.

Most critical scholars think the prayer, especially verses 44–53, was written or expanded by the Deuteronomistic historian in the exile. Jon Levenson argued that the prayer turns the temple into a house of prayer that can be faced from anywhere, which prepared the way for the synagogue.

settings.to: the whole assembly of Israel
settings.when: when he rises from his knees after the prayer
settings.why: Solomon blesses the LORD for giving his people rest and keeping every word he spoke through Moses. He asks God to stay with them and bend their hearts to keep his commands, so that all the earth will know "the LORD is God." He also calls the people to wholehearted loyalty. The blessing makes the temple a call to obedience for Israel and a witness to the nations.

traditions.q: Solomon prays that there is no one who does not sin (1 Kings 8:46). Can a Christian be free from sin in this life?
views: Grace can make a person truly holy, as the saints show. But the Council of Trent taught that no one can avoid all sins, even small (venial) ones, through a whole life without a special gift from God, such as the Church holds of Mary (Session 6, canon 23).

No. Luther taught that a Christian is righteous and a sinner at the same time: fully forgiven and counted righteous for Christ's sake, while sin still clings to him until death. Growth in holiness is real, but it is never complete here.

No. The Westminster Confession says that sanctification is imperfect in this life and that some corruption remains in every part, so a lifelong war goes on (13.2). Solomon's words are true of every believer.

Wesley taught that God can make believers perfect in love in this life, so that they no longer sin on purpose. In his sermon Christian Perfection (1741) he answered this very verse: it described life under the old covenant, while those born of God now do not go on sinning (1 John 5:18). Even the perfect, he said, still make mistakes and need Christ's atonement.
